prime.problem: Published speedups range from 2× to 36.9× for what sounds like the same idea, and every vendor has a headline number. Without a way to place each system on the stack and read its baseline, you copy the wrong design at the wrong scale.
prime.fits: Second-to-last card, after the whole system is drawn. It checks the course's design against what vLLM, SGLang, TGI, TensorRT-LLM and thirteen production teams actually built, using the same seven scheduler choices and the same stack layers.
expect: five engines on seven scheduler choices
recurring patterns: paging, prefix routing, P/D, early rejection
prime.goal: Place any serving system on the stack, compare engines on admission, preemption, prefix caching and chunking, and read a published speedup critically by its baseline, model and workload.

attend: Every engine converged on the same core. Where exactly do they still differ?
Why does TGI never preempt, and what does it pay for that?
vLLM is 24× faster than HF and 3.5× faster than TGI in the same post. What does that tell you about headline speedups?
Which of the recurring patterns only appear at fleet scale, and why not on one box?
Which numbers on this card are vendor or commissioned benchmarks?

must: Every serious engine batches at the iteration level over a paged KV cache with prefix reuse → they differ in how bravely they admit (optimistic, estimate, reserve) and what they do when memory runs out (recompute newest, retract least progress, never preempt)

Above the engine, big fleets add the same layers → a router that sends requests to their prefix, separate prefill and decode pools, KV tiers down to disk, and a gateway that rejects early → each appears only when scale demands it

A speedup = new ÷ baseline, on some model, hardware and workload → the same system looks 3.5× or 24× depending on the baseline → compare only within one setup, prefer "within SLO" claims, and flag vendor numbers
elevated: Reserve-to-completion (TGI, TensorRT-LLM default) never preempts but holds max_new_tokens for every request → when most answers stop early the batch stays small → optimistic admission (vLLM) packs more at the cost of preemption
reference: each engine's commit hash and exact default values
the ByteByteGo post list and dates

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the five-layer stack (gateway, router, pools, engine, KV tiers) and write two real systems on each layer. Then fill a 3-column mini-table for vLLM, SGLang and TGI: admission, preemption, prefix caching.
checklist: engine layer: vLLM, SGLang, TGI, TensorRT-LLM all continuous + paged
admission: vLLM optimistic, SGLang estimate (new_token_ratio), TGI reserve
preemption: vLLM recompute newest, SGLang retract least progress, TGI never
prefix: vLLM chained hashes, SGLang radix tree
fleet layers: llm-d/SGLang router, DeepSeek/Mooncake P/D, Mooncake/GKE early rejection

retrieve.q: Explain why the published continuous-batching speedups range from 2× to 36.9× even though they describe the same idea.
answer: each divides by a different baseline (naive static, optimised static, dynamic, a continuous engine)
models, hardware and output-length spreads differ; bigger models and longer outputs make static look worse
some compare at equal latency, others at peak tok/s

retrieve.q: Walk through what SGLang does when it runs out of KV memory, from admission estimate to victim to recovery.
answer: running requests reserve new_token_ratio × remaining tokens; the ratio starts at 0.7 and decays
when memory runs out it retracts: fewest output tokens first, ties by longest input
the victim is re-prefilled later, and the ratio jumps back up from what was observed

retrieve.q: You run one H100 for an internal chat tool. Which ideas from the case studies do you copy, and which do you skip?
answer: copy the shared core: continuous batching, paged KV, prefix caching, chunked prefill, recompute on preemption
skip P/D pools (nothing to split), fleet routers and KV tiers
add a bounded queue and 429s if load can exceed the replica

compare.q: The full-system card is one reference design; this card is many real ones. Which design choice in the reference would DeepSeek, Character.AI and TGI each change, and why?
answer: DeepSeek: split prefill and decode into separate pools (4 + 18 nodes) and cache KV on disk
Character.AI: sticky sessions and a host-memory KV cache because conversations are long
TGI: reserve to completion instead of preempting

compare.q: Course 5 opens vLLM and SGLang's process structure. Which differences on this card's engine table come from the scheduler, and which from the process layout?
answer: scheduler: decode-first vs prefill-first, optimistic vs estimated admission, recompute vs retract
process layout: where detokenizing runs, overlap scheduling (SGLang on by default)
both engines share continuous batching over paged KV and prefix reuse

predict.q: A new engine claims "20× throughput over Hugging Face Transformers". Before looking up anything: what three questions do you ask, and roughly where would you expect it to land against vLLM?
predict.answer: Ask the baseline (HF generate is a naive, essentially static baseline), the model and hardware, and whether it's peak tok/s or within an SLO. vLLM itself reported 24× over HF and 3.5× over TGI in the same post, so 20× over HF says little: it is likely in the same range as vLLM, not ahead of it. Only a same-setup comparison against a modern continuous engine would tell you more.

apply.task: Two checks on published numbers. (a) DeepSeek reports about 73.7k input tok/s per prefill node and 14.8k output tok/s per decode node, 8 H800s each. Compute tokens per second per GPU for each phase and the ratio. (b) ByteByteGo's tier mix sends 85% to a small model (1/20 of premium cost), 10% to medium (1/5) and 5% to premium, for about 11% of premium cost. Recompute the average cost for a 70% / 20% / 10% mix.
apply.done: (a) ≈ 9,212 input tok/s per prefill GPU vs 1,850 output tok/s per decode GPU, about 5× apart: the same prefill/decode gap the course models on one GPU, now visible in pool sizes. (b) 0.7 × 1/20 + 0.2 × 1/5 + 0.1 × 1 = 0.035 + 0.04 + 0.1 = 0.175 → 17.5% of premium cost.
apply.hint: Divide each node figure by 8; the premium share dominates the tier mix.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: where a "20× over HF" engine lands?
